parts.title: Helping maize take up more phosphorus with the best mixes of strong and weak phosphorus fertilizers
parts.abstract:
Abstract

Phosphorus (P) is a nutrient that every plant needs to grow. Fertilizers that are packed with a lot of phosphorus, which we call high-concentration fertilizers, are crucial for crop growth. But fertilizers that hold less phosphorus, such as calcium magnesium phosphate (CMP) and single super phosphate (SSP), can also be good sources of phosphorus. This is especially true when they are mixed with high-concentration fertilizers like diammonium phosphate (DAP) or monoammonium phosphate (MAP).

In this study, we ran a 48-day experiment in pots to find out how mixing in low-phosphorus fertilizers could help maize make the best use of phosphorus. In acidic soil, we used CMP to replace some of the DAP. In alkaline soil, we used SSP to replace some of the MAP. We tested five different mixes of SSP and MAP, and five mixes of CMP and DAP. We measured how much the plants grew above ground (the shoots) and below ground (the roots), how much phosphorus the shoots took up, how long the roots grew, and how much of the soil's phosphorus was in a form plants could use.

In acidic soil, maize given 100% DAP grew about as much and took up about as much phosphorus as maize given 50% CMP and 50% DAP. In alkaline soil, we saw the same pattern: 100% MAP gave similar results to 50% SSP and 50% DAP. Roots were heaviest and longest with 100% MAP in acidic soil and with 100% DAP in alkaline soil. When we replaced half of the MAP with SSP, or half of the DAP with CMP, root weight and length showed no statistically significant differences. (A difference is called statistically significant when a gap that large would rarely appear by chance alone if there were really no difference. "Not significant" means we could not show a difference, not that there is none.)

Replacing half of the MAP with SSP, or half of the DAP with CMP, also raised the amount and share of the soil's easily released inorganic phosphorus. This is the phosphorus that dissolves in water (H2O-Pi) or in a mild baking-soda solution (NaHCO3-Pi). It had a direct, positive effect on Olsen-P, a standard measure of how much phosphorus in the soil is available to plants.

Our findings show that 1:1 blends of SSP and MAP in acidic soil, and of CMP and DAP in alkaline soil, meet maize's phosphorus needs well without relying only on high-concentration fertilizers. This shows that mixing fertilizers carefully can make the best use of phosphorus, which is crucial for farming that can last into the future.

Keywords: phosphorus, maize, inorganic phosphorus pool, alkaline soil, acidic soil
parts.introduction_first:
Phosphorus (P) is a nutrient that every crop needs, and a shortage of it is one of the main things that limits how much food farms can produce (Raymond et al., 2021; Janes-Bassett et al., 2022). Farmers have used phosphorus fertilizers to raise the amount of phosphorus in the soil that plants can use, to grow bigger harvests, and to plan how much phosphorus fertilizer to apply (Gong et al., 2022a; Yan et al., 2022).

High-concentration fertilizers, such as monoammonium phosphate (MAP) and diammonium phosphate (DAP), dissolve easily in water. Because of this, they can quickly release phosphorus into the water held in the soil, where plant roots can take it up (Chien et al., 2011). However, earlier studies have shown that crops do not always need phosphorus that dissolves so easily (Chien et al., 2009). Our own earlier work also suggested that fertilizers with little phosphorus can be added to fertilizer blends to help crops make better use of the phosphorus they receive (Gong et al., 2022a).

Researchers have tried to work out a good ratio of low-phosphorus to high-phosphorus fertilizers for growing crops. For example, plants took up much more phosphorus when DAP was mixed with phosphate rock, a natural mineral, in a ratio of 1 part DAP to 4 parts phosphate rock by phosphorus (Bindraban et al., 2020). In another study, wheat took up the most phosphorus when struvite, a mineral that can be recovered from wastewater, was mixed with DAP in ratios of 20:80 and 10:90, compared with using only struvite or only DAP. This showed that the best blend contained less struvite than the easily dissolving DAP or MAP (Talboys et al., 2016).

Even with all this work, it is still unclear which ratios of low- to high-phosphorus fertilizers make the best use of phosphorus and help plants grow. Our research aims to fill this gap by finding the best blend ratios of low- and high-phosphorus fertilizers so that crops make the most of the phosphorus they are given.
parts.conclusion:
5.

Conclusion

We tested blends of SSP with MAP, and blends of CMP with DAP, to see which ones helped maize grow as well as possible. SSP and CMP on their own were not enough to keep maize growing well. However, maize grew about as well when we replaced up to 50% of the MAP with SSP in acidic soil, and up to 50% of the DAP with CMP in alkaline soil. This shows that the weaknesses of the high-phosphorus fertilizers (MAP and DAP) can be made up for by mixing them with low-phosphorus fertilizers.

Replacing up to 50% of the MAP with SSP in acidic soil, and up to 50% of the DAP with CMP in alkaline soil, can meet the crop's need for phosphorus. These findings give a starting point for choosing the right kinds of phosphorus fertilizer when growing maize, so that crops make better use of it. Future research could fine-tune these blend ratios for different kinds of soil, so that maize gets the phosphorus it needs. This kind of fine-tuning not only helps maize make better use of phosphorus. It also supports farming that can last into the future, because it means relying less on high-concentration phosphorus fertilizers. It gives a solid base for future studies that aim to choose the best phosphorus fertilizers for maize, and so it contributes a great deal to farming that is both sustainable and efficient.
parts.introduction_rest:
DAP and MAP are packed with phosphorus, and plants can take up this phosphorus easily. This can help roots get started early and help young seedlings grow (Nziguheba et al., 2016; Gong et al., 2022b). Later on, it can also help plants take up more phosphorus from a low-phosphorus fertilizer that has been treated with acid (Geissler et al., 2019; Weeks et al., 2023). Because the high-concentration fertilizer keeps releasing phosphorus over time, the plant gets a steady supply through its whole growing season.

Phosphorus does not stay in one form in the soil. It changes a great deal, both physically and chemically. It can dissolve into the water in the soil, or it can come out of the water as a solid. It can also stick to the surfaces of soil particles, or come loose from them again (Ghodszad et al., 2022; Zheng et al., 2023). Together, these changes keep the soil's phosphorus in a complicated balance between its different forms.

To understand this balance, scientists usually split the soil's phosphorus into several groups, called fractions. Each fraction is a different "pool" of phosphorus, and the fractions change into one another over time (Kim et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2020). We expect the amount of phosphorus that plants can use to go up as stable, tightly held phosphorus turns into easily released forms. This can happen while roots are getting started, and again after a low-phosphorus fertilizer treated with acid is added (Chen et al., 2021; Joshi et al., 2021).

More research is needed to find out how blends of low- and high-phosphorus fertilizers interact with the different pools of soil phosphorus, and which blend ratios work best for growing crops. This could help us predict more accurately how much of the soil's phosphorus plants can use, and help farmers manage soil phosphorus better.

In the past, plans for using phosphorus fertilizer have mostly relied on mineral phosphorus, especially from high-concentration fertilizers such as DAP and MAP. However, relying on these fertilizers may mean that crops make poor use of the phosphorus they are given. It may also raise the risk that phosphorus is lost from the field and pollutes rivers, lakes and other waters (Bindraban et al., 2020; Weeks and Hettiarachchi, 2019). So it is very important to find better ways of managing high-concentration phosphorus fertilizers.

One good way is to blend a high-concentration fertilizer, such as MAP or DAP, with a fertilizer that holds less phosphorus. The aim is to give the crop enough phosphorus early in the season. At the same time, it lowers the risk of pollution that comes from high-concentration fertilizers dissolving so quickly (Everaert et al., 2018). This can help crops make better use of phosphorus. If we measure how each crop responds to different amounts of low-phosphorus fertilizer in the blend, we could find the ratios of low- to high-phosphorus fertilizer that let the crop grow as well as possible.

For these reasons, we ran an experiment in pots with three aims. First, we wanted to measure how different ratios of low- and high-phosphorus fertilizer blends affect how much maize grows and how much phosphorus it takes up, in soils with different levels of acidity (pH), so that we could find the best blend ratios. Second, we wanted to find out how these best blends change the way phosphorus moves between the soil's pools. Third, we wanted to explore ways of using low-phosphorus fertilizer well in blends, so that maize takes up more phosphorus. Our findings can serve as a guide for planning how to use phosphorus fertilizer efficiently, so that phosphorus is used as well as possible.
parts.methods:
2.

Materials and methods

2.1.

How we set up the experiment

We ran a pot experiment with maize from May to July 2022 in a greenhouse at the Quzhou Experimental Station of China Agricultural University, in Quzhou County, Hebei Province, China.

We collected two kinds of soil. The alkaline soil came from Quzhou (Hebei Province). Its pH, measured in water, was 8.13. It held 9.69 g of organic carbon and 1.10 g of total nitrogen in every kilogram of soil. It also held 2.49 mg of Olsen-P and 183 mg of available potassium in every kilogram. The acidic red soil came from Yuxi (Yunnan Province). Its pH, measured in water, was 5.34. It held 3.85 g of organic carbon and 0.80 g of total nitrogen in every kilogram of soil. It also held 1.42 mg of Olsen-P and 153 mg of available potassium in every kilogram. We dried both soils in the air and passed them through a sieve with 2-mm holes.

For the acidic red soil, we set up one control group and five treatment groups. The control group (CK) got no phosphorus. The five treatments were 100% calcium magnesium phosphate (100% CMP), 30% CMP with 70% DAP (30% CMP+70% DAP), 50% CMP with 50% DAP (50% CMP+50% DAP), 70% CMP with 30% DAP (70% CMP+30% DAP), and 100% DAP (100% DAP).

The alkaline soil had the same setup: one control group and five treatments. Here the control group (CK) got no phosphorus. The five treatments were 100% single superphosphate (100% SSP), 30% SSP with 70% MAP (30% SSP+70% MAP), 50% SSP with 50% MAP (50% SSP+50% MAP), 70% SSP with 30% MAP (70% SSP+30% MAP), and 100% MAP (100% MAP).

Each of the six treatments in each soil had four replicates, meaning four pots given the same treatment. That made 48 pots in total. We placed the pots in a completely randomized design, so that chance alone decided where each pot went. This helps make sure that small differences in light or warmth across the greenhouse do not line up with one treatment.

Each pot received 150 kg of phosphorus per hectare (kg P ha-1) of its fertilizer blend. In the pots that got fertilizer, we also added urea as a source of nitrogen and muriate of potash as a source of potassium. We applied nitrogen (N) and potassium (K₂O) at 150 kg per hectare each (Table 1). At planting, we mixed all the fertilizers completely into the soil.

We used maize seeds of the variety Zhengdan958 (Zea mays L. cv. Zhengdan958). First, we cleaned the outside of the seeds to kill any germs on them. We soaked them in 10% hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) for 30 minutes, then rinsed them three times with deionized water, which is very pure water with its dissolved minerals removed. Next, we soaked the seeds for 1 day in a supersaturated calcium sulfate (CaSO4) solution, a liquid holding as much calcium sulfate as it can dissolve. We then let them sprout for 3 days at 25°C in a dish lined with wet filter paper, under a cover that let air in. We picked seeds that had sprouted evenly and sowed them in the pots.

Every day, we weighed the pots and watered them until they held 80% of the most water the soil could hold after draining (80% field capacity). The greenhouse was 20°C at night and 30°C during the day.

2.2.

Harvesting the plants and testing the samples

We harvested the maize plants after eight weeks. We separated the shoots from the roots. We dried the shoots in an oven at 105°C for half an hour, then at 75°C for 4 days, until their weight stopped changing. We weighed the dry samples, crushed them, and mixed them well.

To measure phosphorus, we first had to break the plant material down completely. We dried each part of the plant and then dissolved the ground samples in a mixture of sulfuric acid and hydrogen peroxide (H2SO4-H2O2), following the method of Wolf (1982). We measured the phosphorus in these liquids with the standard vanadomolybdate method (Murphy and Riley, 1962). In this test, a chemical turns the liquid yellow, and the deeper the yellow, the more phosphorus there is. We worked out how much phosphorus the shoots took up from the dry weights and phosphorus levels of the different plant parts.

We carefully pulled the roots out of the soil and shook off any loose soil. We collected every root we could see in each pot, lifting it out of the soil onto a mesh with 2-mm holes. In the lab, we washed the roots under running water until they were clean. We spread the roots on a clear tray with water and scanned them at 400 dpi with an EPSON scanner (Epson Expression 1600 pro, Model EU-35, Japan). We used the WinRHIZO software (Pro2004b, version 5.0; Regent Instruments Inc., QC, Canada) to measure the total root length from the images. Finally, we dried the roots in an oven and weighed them to find their weight.

We dried the soil samples in the open air and passed them through a sieve with 2-mm holes. We broke the soil down with sulfuric acid (H2SO4) and perchloric acid (HClO4). We then measured its total phosphorus with an ultraviolet spectrometer (UV 2500, Shimadzu, Tokyo, Japan), an instrument that measures how much light a liquid absorbs.

To measure Olsen-P, we pulled phosphorus out of the soil with a baking-soda solution (NaHCO3) and used molybdenum blue colorimetry. This test turns the liquid blue, and the deeper the blue, the more phosphorus there is.

We also measured the different forms of phosphorus in the soil, using methods adapted from Hedley et al. (1982) and Sui et al. (1999). We washed the soil with a series of liquids, one after another, each pulling out a different form of phosphorus. We used deionized water to pull out the phosphorus that dissolves in water (H2O-Pi). We used 0.5 M NaHCO3 to pull out the phosphorus that dissolves in a mild baking-soda solution (NaHCO3-Pi). We used 0.1 M NaOH to pull out the next form (NaOH-Pi), and 1 M HCl to pull out the last form (HCl-Pi). (M, or molar, is a measure of how strong a solution is.) After all these steps, we dissolved whatever phosphorus was left in the soil with H2SO4-H2O2 and measured it.

2.3.

How we analyzed the data

We did our statistics with IBM SPSS Statistics 20 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA). We used a one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) to compare the six phosphorus treatments. This test checks whether the averages of several groups differ by more than chance alone would usually produce. We followed it with Tukey's test, which shows which particular pairs of treatments differ. We called a difference statistically significant when p < 0.05. This means that if there were really no difference, a gap that large would appear by chance alone less than 5% of the time.

We compared shoot weight, the phosphorus the shoots took up, root weight, root length, and the different forms of phosphorus in the soil. We also used simple path analysis in IBM SPSS Statistics 20 to look at which measurements affected shoot weight. This method traces how one measurement may be linked to another, step by step. We drew our charts with Sigmaplot 10.0 (version 10.0; Systat Software Inc., San Jose, CA, USA).
parts.results:
3.

Results

3.1.

How much the shoots grew and how much phosphorus they took up

The blends of CMP and DAP in acidic soil, and the blends of SSP and MAP in alkaline soil, affected plant growth in clearly different ways depending on the crop (Figure 1). In both soils, every plant that got phosphorus fertilizer grew more than the plants in the control treatment (CK), which got no added phosphorus. This confirms that maize in the control soil was short of phosphorus, and that the differences in growth we saw came from how much phosphorus was available.

The more of the blend was made up of MAP or DAP, the heavier the shoots tended to be. In acidic soil, maize given 100% DAP had the heaviest shoots. Maize given 50% CMP and 50% DAP, and maize given 30% CMP and 70% DAP, did not differ significantly from each other. Both of these blends, however, gave significantly heavier shoots than 100% CMP or the control. In alkaline soil, the shoots ranked from heaviest to lightest like this: 100% MAP, then 30% SSP and 70% MAP, then 50% SSP and 50% MAP, then 70% SSP and 30% MAP, then 100% SSP, and finally the control.

Figure 1

How well the plants grew (A) and how much their shoots weighed (B) under each phosphorus fertilizer treatment in acidic soil. The same two measurements (C and D) under each treatment in alkaline soil. Treatments marked with different lowercase letters are significantly different from each other (p < 0.05). This means that if there were really no difference, a gap this large would appear by chance alone less than 5% of the time.

The amount of phosphorus the shoots took up followed the same pattern as shoot weight (Figure 2). In acidic soil, maize given 100% DAP took up 77.4% more phosphorus in total than maize given 100% CMP. In alkaline soil, maize given 100% MAP took up 42.1% more phosphorus in total than maize given 100% SSP.

Interestingly, in acidic soil, maize given 50% CMP and 50% DAP did not take up significantly more phosphorus than maize given 100% DAP. In alkaline soil, maize given 50% SSP and 50% MAP took up no different amount of phosphorus from maize given 100% MAP. Taken together, these results suggest that the amount of phosphorus the shoots took up was closely linked to how much the shoots grew.

Figure 2

How much phosphorus the shoots took up under each phosphorus fertilizer treatment in acidic (A) and alkaline (B) soil. We first used a test called one-way ANOVA, which checks whether the averages of several groups differ by more than chance would explain. We then used Duncan's multiple range test to compare the treatments pair by pair. Treatments marked with different lowercase letters are significantly different (p < 0.05).

3.2.

Root weight and root length

The phosphorus supplied by the soil had a significant effect on the shape and size of the roots, in both the acidic and the alkaline soil. In acidic soil, the heaviest roots came from three treatments: 50% CMP and 50% DAP, 30% CMP and 70% DAP, and 100% DAP. Compared with the control, these gave roots that were 85.4%, 86.0% and 86.3% heavier (Figure 3A). Next came 70% CMP and 30% DAP and 100% CMP, whose roots were also significantly heavier than the control's.

In alkaline soil, the roots were significantly heavier with 100% MAP, 30% SSP and 70% MAP, and 50% SSP and 50% MAP than with 70% SSP and 30% MAP or 100% SSP. The three MAP-based treatments did not differ significantly from one another (Figure 3B). In acidic soil, the roots with 50% CMP and 50% DAP weighed about the same as those with 100% DAP. In alkaline soil, the roots with 50% SSP and 50% MAP did not differ significantly in weight from those with 100% MAP.

Figure 3

Root weight under each phosphorus fertilizer treatment in acidic (A) and alkaline (B) soil. Root length under each treatment in acidic (C) and alkaline (D) soil. Treatments marked with different lowercase letters are significantly different (p < 0.05), using Duncan's multiple range test after a significant one-way ANOVA.

Root length told a similar story to root weight. In acidic soil, the average root length was 59.1 cm with 50% CMP and 50% DAP, 61.4 cm with 30% CMP and 70% DAP, and 62.7 cm with 100% DAP. These roots were significantly longer than those with 70% CMP and 30% DAP or 100% CMP. The roots with 50% CMP and 50% DAP and those with 100% DAP did not differ significantly in weight.

In alkaline soil, the roots with 100% MAP were only 8% longer than those with 50% SSP and 50% MAP, and the difference in length between these two treatments was not significant (Figures 3C, D).

3.3.

The different forms of phosphorus in the soil

We split the soil's inorganic phosphorus into four parts, called fractions, using a standard method known as the Hedley method. Each fraction is released by a different chemical wash, so each one shows how tightly the phosphorus is held in the soil. The water fraction (H2O-Pi) is the most easily released. Next comes the fraction released by a mild baking-soda solution (NaHCO3-Pi), then one released by a strong alkali (NaOH-Pi), and finally one released by hydrochloric acid (HCl-Pi). Whatever is left over is called residual phosphorus.

When the blend contained more than 50% MAP or DAP, the blends of CMP and DAP in acidic soil, and the blends of SSP and MAP in alkaline soil, significantly increased the water, baking-soda, alkali and acid fractions (Table 2). In acidic soil, the 100% DAP treatment had the most inorganic phosphorus in the soil. The 50% CMP and 50% DAP and 30% CMP and 70% DAP treatments did not differ significantly from each other, but both had significantly more than the CMP-only and control treatments. Compared with the control, the 50% CMP and 50% DAP treatment raised the water fraction by 415%, the baking-soda fraction by 160.4% and the alkali fraction by 82.8%.

In alkaline soil, the 100% MAP treatment also had the most inorganic phosphorus, but it did not differ significantly from the 50% SSP and 50% MAP treatment. Compared with the control, the 50% SSP and 50% MAP treatment raised the water fraction by 142.8%, the baking-soda fraction by 265.8% and the alkali fraction by 36.5%.

Figure 4 shows a path coefficient structural model. This is a diagram that uses arrows to show how strongly each measurement is linked to the others, and which way the link runs. The phosphorus fertilizers in both the 50% CMP and 50% DAP and the 50% SSP and 50% MAP treatments increased the water fraction, which in turn led to more phosphorus being available in the soil. In the same way, adding phosphorus fertilizer in these treatments increased the alkali fraction. The positive arrows in the diagram show that this fraction also made a significant contribution to the overall amount of phosphorus available to plants (Olsen-P).

parts.discussion:
4.

Discussion

4.1.

Matching the fertilizer to the soil so that phosphorus is used well

In our study, maize grew significantly more in total when a large share of the fertilizer was MAP or DAP (Figure 1). This agrees with earlier studies, which stress that a balanced supply of nutrients is important for getting the most out of a crop (Gong et al., 2024). Maize may respond more strongly to MAP or DAP because these are high-concentration fertilizers. They can supply enough phosphorus to help young roots get started (Chien et al., 2011).

As we expected, roots were heaviest and longest in two treatments: 100% DAP in acidic soil, and 100% MAP in alkaline soil. This shows how important a well-grown root system is for taking up phosphorus and for reaching a good harvest. The reason is that phosphorus moves very little through soil (Flaval et al., 2014; Hertzberger et al., 2021).

Adding high-concentration fertilizers such as MAP or DAP is an efficient way to raise the amount of phosphorus in the soil that plants can use. These fertilizers dissolve easily in water, so when moisture starts to dissolve the fertilizer granules, phosphorus moves into the water held in the soil (Weeks and Hettiarachchi, 2019).

However, adding a lot of high-phosphorus fertilizer does not necessarily mean maize will keep producing bigger harvests. An earlier study found that when plants were grown close together, low-phosphorus fertilizers (SSP or CMP) gave bigger harvests than high-phosphorus fertilizers (MAP or DAP) (Gong et al., 2022b). Once high-concentration fertilizers are added to soil, they quickly become much less able to dissolve in water. This happens because the soil "fixes" the phosphorus, meaning it locks it up so that plants can take up less of it (Feng et al., 2019; Maharajan et al., 2021). So it is essential to work out the best blend of phosphorus fertilizers. A good blend helps turn phosphorus that dissolves poorly into forms plants can use, and helps crops make efficient use of it.

4.2.

Ways to manage phosphorus so that crops use it better

New approaches, such as mixing high- and low-phosphorus fertilizers, can make soil microbes more active. This helps turn phosphorus that dissolves easily into forms plants can use. To get the most out of blended fertilizers and support farming that can last into the future, farmers need to think carefully about the soil, what the crop needs, and the surrounding environment.

In our pot experiments, two blends significantly improved how much phosphorus the plants took up. In alkaline soil, this was 50% MAP mixed with 50% SSP. In acidic soil, it was 50% DAP mixed with 50% CMP. The phosphorus taken up by these blends was not significantly different from that taken up by 100% MAP and 100% DAP, but it was greater than in the control treatment (CK), the untreated comparison. This suggests that the blends gave the plants about as much phosphorus as the pure high-concentration fertilizers.

DAP is a high-concentration fertilizer made by treating ammonia with phosphoric acid. In acidic soil, iron (Fe) and aluminium (Al) play a big part in limiting how much phosphorus plants can use. Because DAP releases phosphate quickly, it can help plants hold more phosphorus while they are seedlings and while they are tillering, the stage when the plant sends out extra side shoots (Ma et al., 2023; Ning et al., 2023). However, earlier studies have shown that this quick release can lead to phosphorus being fixed by iron and aluminium in acidic soil. As a result, the phosphorus fails to meet the plant's needs later in the season (Chien et al., 2011; Ma et al., 2022).

MAP, by contrast, is a slow-acting source of phosphorus. It dissolves well in acidic soil and supplies enough phosphorus later in the season (Gong et al., 2022b; Qin et al., 2022). In our results, the shoots were heaviest and took up the most phosphorus with 100% DAP. However, this was not significantly different from 50% CMP mixed with 50% DAP. This points to a notable rise in phosphorus uptake with the blend, because DAP makes the soil more acidic, and this helps CMP work.

In alkaline soils, MAP is a fertilizer of medium acidity that makes more phosphorus available to plants. The ammonium in MAP lowers the pH (makes the soil more acidic) in the rhizosphere, the thin layer of soil right around the roots. This reduces how much phosphate gets fixed, and it encourages roots to grow, which is vital for taking up phosphate (Nunes et al., 2022).

In our experiments, SSP always left less available phosphorus in the soil than MAP did, and it could not meet the plants' needs in the early stages of growth. With a similar supply of phosphorus, the shoots were significantly heavier and took up significantly more phosphorus with 100% MAP than with 100% SSP. Surprisingly, the shoots with 100% DAP were not significantly different in weight or phosphorus uptake from those given 50% CMP mixed with 50% DAP.

Pairing MAP with SSP is therefore a good way, both for the crop and for the farmer's budget, to supply the phosphorus plants need. MAP can feed the plants early in their development, which leads to better root growth. SSP costs less, so it is a cheaper option that can help lower overall fertilizer costs while still giving crops enough phosphorus. For these reasons, it can be used more effectively in alkaline soils (Gong et al., 2022b).

4.3.

Blends of low- and high-phosphorus fertilizers increased the easily released and moderately released inorganic phosphorus in the soil

Earlier studies have shown that adding phosphorus fertilizer directly changes the different forms of inorganic phosphorus in the soil (Yan et al., 2017). We sorted the soil's inorganic phosphorus into groups by how easily it can be washed out. The first group dissolves in water (H2O-Pi). The second dissolves in a mild baking-soda solution (NaHCO3-Pi). The third dissolves in a strong alkali, sodium hydroxide (NaOH-Pi). The fourth dissolves in hydrochloric acid (HCl-Pi). Whatever is left over is called residual P.

Our results showed that adding chemical phosphorus fertilizers increased the soil's inorganic phosphorus. In the 50% CMP + 50% DAP treatment (acidic soil) and the 50% SSP + 50% MAP treatment (alkaline soil), larger shares of the phosphorus were in the H2O-Pi, NaHCO3-Pi and NaOH-Pi groups, which plants can use. The easily released groups, such as H2O-Pi and NaHCO3-Pi, are direct sources of phosphorus for crops. This shows that the phosphorus added in these two treatments stayed in the forms that are easier to extract (Yan et al., 2022). The NaOH-Pi group was also a major store of phosphorus, and it grew larger when high-phosphorus fertilizers were added.

Under the conditions of our study, HCl-Pi was also an important source of phosphorus for maize in these two treatments, alongside H2O-Pi, NaHCO3-Pi and NaOH-Pi. HCl-Pi and residual P hold phosphorus in a stable form that plants use poorly. Even so, plants can take up more of this phosphorus by changing the shape and workings of their roots, and by using microbes to make insoluble phosphorus dissolve (Shen et al., 2011; Yan et al., 2022).

In this study, the amount of phosphorus fertilizer we recommend met the needs for the best crop growth. Using a suitable ratio of high- to low-phosphorus fertilizers made more of the soil's phosphorus available, which helped roots grow. When roots grow more, they release more organic acids and make the soil around them more acidic. This can unlock soil phosphorus and turn insoluble phosphorus into easily released forms (H2O-Pi and NaHCO3-Pi) (Alamgir et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2023).

For these reasons, ways of managing phosphorus fertilizer should take better account of the soil's conditions. Improving how well soil and plants share phosphorus should also include a set of strategies: helping crops take up more phosphorus, cutting down on the overuse of high-concentration fertilizers, and improving the phosphorus content of low-phosphorus fertilizers.
